chunks: Reducing body diode effects. The question: What can you do to decrease the effect of the internal body diode?
To reduce body-diode effects, you attack them in order of cost. First, shorten the time the diode conducts.
Then bypass it with a faster diode, choose a transistor with less stored charge, and soften the spike. Each step cuts either the wasted power or the ringing.
Go back to the narrow side door. The cheapest fix is to spend less time in it, so you shorten the wait. The next is to add a wider door beside it.
The last is to slow the rush when the main door reopens, so nobody is hurt. The wider door only helps if it is right next to the narrow one, because distance adds delay.
Each curve counts only the dead-time related terms (shoot-through not shown). The silicon body diode is the most expensive at moderate dead time because of recovery charge.
The GaN curve starts at zero but climbs steeply: at 10 nanoseconds it is cheaper than silicon (30 vs 58 milliwatts) but above 50 nanoseconds it is about the same as silicon (150 vs 184 milliwatts).
Adaptive dead time: a gap that the controller shrinks to the smallest safe value. Schottky diode: a diode with a low drop and almost no stored charge.
Reverse-recovery charge ( Q rr ): the stored charge that makes a spike on turn-off ("Design considerations from body diode behavior").
Snubber: a small resistor and capacitor that damps ringing. Loop inductance: the unwanted inductance in the current path, which slows handoffs.
In a 2 amps, 500 kilohertz buck with a 0. 75 volts body-diode drop, 50 nanoseconds of diode conduction per cycle (two dead times added together) wastes about 37. 5 milliwatts.
Cutting the total dead time to 15 nanoseconds cuts that to 0. 75 times 2 times 15 nanoseconds times 500 kilohertz about 11 milliwatts.
The reduction is proportional, and the stored charge falls too. That is the whole idea.
"Attack each mechanism. Shorten the dead time with adaptive control so the diode conducts as little as possible, which cuts both conduction and stored charge.
Add a Schottky in parallel, but only co-packaged or monolithic, since nanohenries of loop inductance stop it taking the current. Choose a FET with low Q rr and soft recovery.
Slow the high-side turn-on or add a snubber and tighten the layout to tame the recovery spike. Or move to GaN, which has no recovery charge but needs very short dead time."
